llm.summary: The skill is mostly a disclosed DingTalk document helper, but it needs review because it can modify cloud documents and its scope conflicts over multidimensional tables and broad node creation.

dimensions.detail: The DINGTALK_MCP_DOCS_URL credential is purpose-aligned and disclosed as a token-bearing URL; local import/export scripts are disclosed and limited to workspace paths, file extensions, and size/content bounds.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The package declares a required mcporter binary and documents global installation with an unpinned lower-bound dependency range, so installed code can change after review; no evidence of malicious install scripts was found in this artifact.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The runtime instructions include state-changing cloud actions, overwrite writes, broad keyword activation, and inconsistent trigger guidance for table and multidimensional table requests, which can route ambiguous user requests to remote resource creation.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No background service, scheduled task, memory poisoning, or backdoor persistence was found; persistence is limited to normal mcporter configuration or environment-variable credential use and global dependency installation.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: Core DingTalk document search, create, read, write, import, and export behavior is coherent, but the top-level description excludes multidimensional table operations while SKILL.md and the API reference instruct creation of multidimensional tables and other node types.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable granting this skill access to a token-bearing DingTalk document service and allowing it to create or overwrite cloud document content. Review ambiguous table or multidimensional-table requests carefully, pin and verify mcporter before global installation, and avoid importing local files unless you have checked their contents and destination.
llm.findings:
[TP4] expected: Local import/export between workspace files and DingTalk docs is real but disclosed in SKILL.md and README, with path and size limits, so this is not hidden exfiltration.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The multidimensional-table and broad node-type creation instructions conflict with the top-level exclusion and are a material scope ambiguity for a state-changing cloud integration.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The table intent rules are inconsistent enough that an agent could create an online table or multidimensional table when the manifest says those requests should not trigger this skill.
[PE3] expected: The /etc/passwd references appear in tests and a test report as blocked traversal cases, not as credential-reading behavior.
[LP3] expected: The skill declares the mcporter binary and DingTalk URL credential, and the shell bridge uses an argument list with shell disabled; local file behavior is documented, though the top-level metadata remains narrower than the full capability set.
[SQP-1] expected: Broad DingTalk document keywords are expected for this skill, but they compound the concern created by state-changing operations and conflicting table scope.
[SQP-2] expected: Remote document creation and writing are central to the stated purpose and are documented, including warnings about overwrite mode and token sensitivity.
[AST4] expected: The subprocess call is an expected mcporter invocation using shell=False and JSON-encoded arguments; I did not find shell-string command injection in the reviewed code.
[SQP-3] expected: Chinese-language documentation is consistent with DingTalk-focused usage and is not treated here as a security concern by itself.
[T08] unexpected: The unpinned global mcporter install is a supply-chain review concern because future accepted versions may differ from the reviewed artifact, though no malicious dependency behavior was found locally.
